items.question: What is the clearest definition of cloud computing from Day 1?
options: Renting compute, storage, and software over the internet instead of owning hardware
Buying physical servers once and keeping them forever in your office
Writing code only on a laptop with no internet connection
Sharing one root password across the whole engineering team
items.ren_hint_english: Think rent vs own — like the electricity grid, not buying a generator.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Rent vs own — electricity grid maadhiri think pannunga, generator vangaadheenga.
items.explanation: Cloud means you rent infrastructure from providers like AWS, GCP, or Azure and pay for what you use. You never buy or maintain the physical machines.

items.question: FoodQuick wants servers close to users in Mumbai. Which AWS Region should they choose?
options: ap-south-1 (Mumbai)
us-east-1 (Virginia)
ap-southeast-1 (Singapore)
eu-west-1 (Ireland)
items.ren_hint_english: Closest Region to Indian users in this lesson was Mumbai.
items.explanation: ap-south-1 is the Mumbai Region. Placing resources near users reduces latency.

items.question: You create an EC2 instance in Mumbai, then a teammate says it is missing. What do you check first?
options: The Region selector in the AWS console
Delete the whole AWS account and start over
Open IAM and disable every user
Assume AWS deleted the instance automatically
items.ren_hint_english: Resources live in the Region you selected — wrong Region looks like missing.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Resource create panna Region-la thaan irukum — wrong Region-la paathaa missing maadhiri theriyum.
items.explanation: Every resource lives in a Region. If the selector is on us-east-1, Mumbai resources will not show. Always check Region first.

items.situation: A friend in Chennai is launching a food delivery app. Traffic is unknown — they might stay small or go viral. A local data center quotes ₹50,000/month for a fixed server.
items.question: What do you recommend, and why?
options: Use AWS — pay for usage and scale up or down as demand changes
Rent the fixed server forever even if usage is near zero
Buy 100 physical servers on day one just in case
Skip servers and store everything only on one phone
items.ren_hint_english: Unpredictable demand + no idle waste = cloud.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Traffic theriyama irukumbodhu — cloud-la pay-for-use + scale best.
items.explanation: Early businesses need elasticity. Cloud avoids paying for idle capacity and can scale in minutes if traffic spikes.

items.situation: A company runs 10 EC2 servers on normal days. On New Year's Eve they expect ~50x traffic for about 4 hours, then back to normal.
items.question: What should they do before midnight and after 4am?
options: Scale up before midnight, then scale back down after the spike
Buy 500 physical servers permanently for one night
Shut everything down before midnight and hope users wait
Change nothing — 10 servers can handle 50x traffic
items.ren_hint_english: Cloud's superpower: temporary capacity with temporary cost.
items.ren_hint_tanglish: Spike-ku scale up, quiet-ku scale down — temporary capacity, temporary cost.
items.explanation: Scale up for the spike, scale down when traffic returns. You pay for the extra capacity only for those hours — not all year.

items.situation: In the AWS console, every resource you create lives in a geographic location AWS calls a Region. Mumbai's Region code was taught today.
items.question: Type the AWS Region code for Mumbai.
items.ren_hint_english: Asia Pacific South, first Region — starts with ap-south.
items.explanation: Mumbai = ap-south-1. Remembering Region codes stops the most common console confusion.
